questions.question: A birth-death queue models the number of jobs $L(t)$ in a system. Which description states the modelling assumption behind it?
options: Jobs may arrive in batches whose rate depends only on the current $L$; given $L=n$, the times are exponential.
Jobs come and go one at a time; given $L=n$, both times to the next event are exponential($\lambda(n)$, $\mu(n)$).
Jobs come and go one at a time; the arrival and departure rates may depend on the whole past path of $L$.
Jobs come and go one at a time; given $L=n$, service may follow any distribution with mean $1/\mu(n)$.

questions.question: An $M/M/1/K$ queue has Poisson arrivals with rate $\lambda$ and room for at most $K$ jobs; $\lambda(n)$ is the arrival rate and $\lambda^+(n)$ the rate at which jobs enter in state $n$. Which values hold at $n=K$?
options: $\lambda(K)=0$ and $\lambda^+(K)=0$
$\lambda(K)=\lambda$ and $\lambda^+(K)=\lambda$
$\lambda(K)=\lambda$ and $\lambda^+(K)=0$
$\lambda(K)=\lambda(1-p(K))$ and $\lambda^+(K)=0$

questions.question: In an $M/M/3$ queue each server finishes a job after an independent exponential time with rate $\mu$. Exactly $n=2$ jobs are present. Why is the departure rate $\mu(2)=2\mu$?
options: Two servers are busy; the minimum of two independent exponential($\mu$) times has rate $2\mu$.
Three servers are available, so the departure rate is $3\mu$ whatever the number of jobs.
Jobs leave one at a time, so the departure rate stays $\mu$ whatever the number of busy servers.
The two jobs share one server, so each runs at half speed and the rate becomes $\mu/2$.

questions.question: In a birth-death queue some arriving jobs are blocked: $\lambda(n)$ is the arrival rate in state $n$, $\lambda^+(n)$ the entering rate, with $\lambda^+(n)<\lambda(n)$ in every blocking state and $\lambda^+(n)=\lambda(n)$ elsewhere, $\mu(n)$ the departure rate and $p(n)$ the stationary probabilities. Which level-crossing equation holds for every $n\geq0$?
options: $\lambda^+(n)p(n)=\mu(n)p(n+1)$
$\lambda(n)p(n)=\mu(n+1)p(n+1)$
$\lambda^+(n)p(n+1)=\mu(n+1)p(n)$
$\lambda^+(n)p(n)=\mu(n+1)p(n+1)$

questions.question: A single-server birth-death queue has $\lambda^+(n)=\lambda$ for $n<K$, $\lambda^+(n)=0$ for $n\geq K$ with finite $K$, and $\mu(n)=\mu$, where $\lambda>\mu$. Which statement about the stationary probabilities $p(n)$ is correct?
options: No stationary probabilities exist, because jobs arrive faster than they are served.
It exists, because the normalising sum has only $K+1$ positive terms.
It exists only after $\lambda$ is lowered below $\mu$.
It exists only if $\lambda<K\mu$, the capacity of $K$ busy servers.

questions.question: A repair shop serves $N=4$ machines; each working machine fails at rate $0.5$ per hour, and $c=2$ mechanics each repair at rate $1$ per hour. With $n=3$ machines in the shop, what are $\lambda^+(3)$ and $\mu(3)$?
A birth-death queue with arrival rate $\lambda$ and service rate $\mu$ per server has $\lambda^+(n)=\lambda\mathbf{1}\{n<4\}$ and $\mu(n)=\mu\min\{n,2\}$. Which Kendall model is this?
A birth-death queue has $\lambda^+(0)=3$, $\lambda^+(1)=2$, $\mu(1)=1$ and $\mu(2)=4$. Using $\lambda^+(n)p(n)=\mu(n+1)p(n+1)$, what is the ratio $p(2)/p(0)$?
A birth-death queue on states $0,1,2$ has $\lambda^+(0)=2$, $\lambda^+(1)=1$, $\lambda^+(2)=0$, $\mu(1)=1$ and $\mu(2)=2$. What is the stationary probability $p(0)$?
An $M/M/1/3$ queue has arrival rate $\lambda=1$ and service rate $\mu=2$, with $p(0)=8/15$, $p(1)=4/15$, $p(2)=2/15$, $p(3)=1/15$. What is the mean acceptance rate $\lambda^+=\sum_n\lambda^+(n)p(n)$?
In a birth-death queue, $p(n)$ is the long-run fraction of time with $n$ jobs and $\pi(n)$ the fraction of arrivals that see $n$ jobs. In which case is $\pi(n)=p(n)$ for all $n$ guaranteed?
options: Whenever the stationary probabilities $p(n)$ exist.
When no job is ever blocked, so that $\lambda^+(n)=\lambda(n)$.
When $\lambda(n)=\lambda$ in every state, including blocking states.
When the departure rate $\mu(n)=\mu$ is the same in every state.

questions.question: A single-server birth-death queue has $\mu(n)=\mu$, Poisson arrivals with rate $\lambda$, and blocks at capacity $K$, so $p(K)>0$. How does the utilisation $1-p(0)$ compare with the load $\rho=\lambda/\mu$?
options: $1-p(0)=\lambda^+/\mu$, which is below $\rho$ because blocked jobs bring no work.
$1-p(0)=\rho$, because each arriving job brings on average $1/\mu$ of work.
$1-p(0)=\lambda^+/\mu$, which is above $\rho$ because accepted jobs find shorter queues.
$1-p(0)=\lambda^+/\mu$ and $\lambda^+=\lambda$, since blocked jobs still count as arrivals.

questions.question: A single server receives Poisson arrivals with rate $\lambda$, but every service takes exactly $1/\mu$ time units. Why is the number of jobs $L(t)$ not a birth-death queue with $\mu(n)=\mu$?
options: The mean service time is not $1/\mu$ once service times are deterministic.
With deterministic service, jobs leave in batches rather than one at a time.
Deterministic service changes the arrivals, which are then no longer Poisson.
Given $L=n$, the time to the next departure depends on how long service has run.

questions.question: A birth-death queue has $\lambda^+(n)=2$ for all $n\geq0$ and $\mu(n)=n$ for $n\geq1$ (each job has its own server with rate $1$). What is the ratio $p(3)/p(0)$?

Three machines each fail at rate $1$ per day while working, and one mechanic repairs at rate $3$, so $\lambda(n)=3-n$ and $\mu(n)=3$. Then $p(0)=p(1)=9/26$, $p(2)=6/26$, $p(3)=2/26$. What fraction $\pi(0)$ of failures find the shop empty?

An $M/M/1/K$ queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=2$ per hour; the system is full with probability $p(K)=0.1$ and the mean number of jobs is $\mathbb{E}[L]=3$. What is the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ of accepted jobs in hours?
A birth-death queue without blocking has step ratios $r_n=\lambda^+(n)/\mu(n+1)$. Does the condition $r_n<1$ for every $n\geq0$ guarantee that stationary probabilities $p(n)$ exist?
options: Yes: then $p(n)$ decreases in $n$, and decreasing probabilities have a finite sum.
Yes: $r_n<1$ is the $M/M/1$ condition $\lambda<\mu$ applied in each state.
No: stationary probabilities also need a finite capacity $K$.
No: $r_n=\frac{n+1}{n+2}$ gives $p(n)=\frac{p(0)}{n+1}$, a divergent sum.

questions.question: In a finite calling population model with $N$ machines, each working machine fails at rate $\lambda$, so the arrival rate of failures in state $n$ is $\lambda(n)=\lambda(N-n)$. Which statement about the arrival process of failures is correct?
options: Failures form a Poisson process with rate $\lambda N$, since each failure is a single birth of the queue.
While the state is $n$ the time to the next failure is exponential($\lambda(N-n)$), so the gaps are not identically distributed.
Failures form a Poisson process whose constant rate is the long-run failure rate $\sum_n\lambda(n)p(n)$.
The time to the next failure is not exponential in any state, so the model is not a birth-death queue.

questions.question: A birth-death queue has $\lambda^+(n)=2$ for all $n\geq0$, $\mu(1)=1$, and $\mu(n)=4$ for $n\geq2$ (a faster mode starts at two jobs). What is $p(0)$?
options: No stationary probabilities, as $\lambda^+(0)>\mu(1)$.

questions.question: Taxis arrive at a hotel as a Poisson process with rate $20$ per hour, parties of riders as one with rate $15$ per hour. A waiting taxi takes an arriving party at once and vice versa; at most $2$ taxis wait, a further taxi leaves. With state $n=2-(\text{taxis waiting})+(\text{parties waiting})$ this is a birth-death queue. What fraction of arriving parties has to wait for a taxi in the long run?
options: No long-run fraction exists: taxis arrive faster than parties, so the queue is unstable.
